column1: # Format: <extended regex><TAB><reason shown to Claude>. Matching is case-insensitive.
# Use POSIX classes ([[:space:]]) so the rules behave the same with GNU and BSD grep.
# This is a guardrail, not a sandbox: it catches mistakes, not a determined attacker.

column2: recursive force delete outside the project (absolute path, ~, $HOME, *, . or ..). Delete explicit paths inside the project instead.
rm with separate -r -f flags (or --no-preserve-root). Delete explicit paths inside the project instead.
writing to a raw device. Never needed for application development.
chmod 777 opens files to everyone. Use the narrowest permission that works (e.g. 755 or 644).
sudo is not allowed for the agent. Ask the human to run privileged commands.
force push rewrites shared history. Use --force-with-lease on your own branch, or ask the human.
git reset --hard throws away uncommitted work. Use git stash, or ask the human.
git clean -f deletes untracked files for good. List them with git clean -n and ask the human.
--no-verify skips the project's checks. Fix the failing check instead.
piping a downloaded script into a shell runs unreviewed code. Download it, read it, then ask the human.
publishing an artifact is a release decision. Ask the human.
pushing images or deleting cluster resources is an operations decision. Ask the human.
destructive SQL. Write a migration (Flyway/Liquibase) and let the human review it.
reading, copying or moving secret files. Use .env.example or ask the human for the value you need.
writing a secret file from the shell. Put placeholders in .env.example and let the human fill the real file.
